title: TA9-01860
frame:
Forum: Refugee Protection Division (first-instance tribunal).
Parties: the claimant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review: none; this is the first-instance decision.
How the layers nest here: The member of the tribunal is the author (layer 1). The claimant and the Minister make submissions to the member (layer 2). There is no earlier decision-maker unless the reasons describe a prior decision (layer 3). Testimony and documents are layer 5.

paragraphs.text: REASONS AND DECISION [1] XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX (hereinafter referred to as the "the claimant") and his spouse, XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX (hereinafter referred to as "XXXXX"), along with their children XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX and XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX (the "minor claimants"), are citizens of Mexico claiming refugee protection under sections 96 and 97(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA).1 These claims were joined according to Rule 49(1) of the Refugee Protection Division Rules. The father of the minor claimant was appointed as her Designated Representative according to section 167(2) of the IRPA. The identities of the claimants as nationals of Mexico is established by true certified copies of their Mexican passports.2 The hearing into these claims for protection was adjourned on December 1, 2009, pending receipt of additional documentation with translation by December 15, 2009. On December 14, 2009, the Board received a declaration with translation from Mrs. XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX, accompanied by a photocopy and translation of Mrs. XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX Federal Electoral Card from Mexico.
The claimant alleges the following:

The claimant alleges a well founded fear of persecution at the hands of Los Zetas, a criminal organization involved in drug trafficking. He was a XXXXX store shopkeeper in Veracruz and was targeted by Los Zetas because they believed that he was passing information about their operations in the area to the Federal police. Los Zetas came to his XXXXX store and threatened to kill him. They also kidnapped him, forced him into their vehicle, and took him to an undisclosed location where they threatened him with death and beat him up. They told him that in order to teach him a lesson for giving information to the police about their operations, he was going to have to give them all of XXXXX XXXXX his business, his car, and his money. They warned him not to go to the police because the police were working in cahoots with them. The claimant never went to the police for assistance because he feared Los Zetas and their corruption. The claimant was forced to relinquish ownership of his vehicle to Los Zetas and to sell off his business and give the proceeds of the sale to them. The claimant left Mexico XXXXX, 2009 and came to Canada. He submitted his claim for protection at Pearson International Airport on January 28, 2009.

I find that the claimants are neither Convention refugees nor persons in need of protection pursuant to sections 96 and 97(1) of the IRPA. The determinative issues in these claims are nexus and state protection. ANALYSIS Section 96 of the IRPA - Convention Refugee Grounds Nexus

The determinative issue in this section 96 analysis is nexus, that is, whether there is a link between the claimants' fear of persecution and any of the Convention grounds. I find that there is no such link.

The claimant testified that he fears Los Zetas, an organization which is involved in criminal activities and drugtrafficking, including corrupt police officers and government officials who colloborate with them. According to the documentary evidence, Los Zetas is one of the enforcer gangs of the Gulf drug cartel in Mexico. The claimant testified that Los Zetas targeted him because they believed he was passing information to the federal police about their drug operations. He testified that members of Los Zetas kidnapped him and threatened to kill him and his children out of revenge for his having given the federal police information about their gang and its activities. The claimant testified that members of the gang told him that they were going to make him pay for having been an informant to the federal police by demanding that he hand over his vehicle, his business, his money, and all the XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX. There is no persuasive evidence to establish that the actions of Los Zetas were in any way motivated by reasons of race, religion, nationality, political opinion, or membership in a particular social group. I find that their motives were purely criminal in nature and that their actions were driven by a personal vendetta they had against the claimant based on their perception that he was feeding the federal authorities information about their gang and activities of their bosses. The Federal Court has held that victims of crime, corruption3 or vendettas4 generally fail to establish a link between their fear of persecution and one of the Convention grounds in the definition of Convention refugee. The Board has been upheld in its finding of lack of nexus, where the claimant was a target of a personal vendetta5 or where the claimant was a victim of crime.6 Therefore, I find that the claimant is a victim of crime and a personal vendetta and that there is no link to any of the Convention grounds. As a result this claim must fail under section 96 of the IRPA. However, a separate analysis under section 97 of the IRPA follows. Section 97 - Persons in Need of Protection State Protection

The determinative issue in this section 97 analysis is whether or not adequate state protection is available to the claimant and his family in Mexico. I find that adequate state protection would be reasonably forthcoming to the claimant and his family if they were to approach the authorities in Mexico for assistance.

In assessing the issue of state protection, I am guided by a number of cases from the Supreme Court of Canada and the Federal Court. In this regard, the courts have established a number of principles relating to state protection and I have applied those principles to the case at hand.

There is a presumption that a state is capable of protecting its citizens except in situations where the state is in a state of a complete breakdown.7 To rebut the presumption of state protection, a claimant must provide clear and convincing evidence of the state's inability to protect, absent an admission by the national's state of its inability to protect that national.8 While the effectiveness of the protection is a relevant consideration, the test is whether the protection offered is adequate.9 The evidence that state protection is not adequate must be reliable and probative and it must also satisfy me, on a balance of probabilities, that the state protection is inadequate.10 The claimant must approach the state for protection, providing that state protection might be reasonably forthcoming.11 Where a state is in effective control of its territory, has military, police and civil authority in place and makes serious efforts to protect its citizens, the mere fact it is not always successful at doing so will not be enough to justify a claim that the victims are unable to avail themselves of protection.12 The fact that state protection is not perfect13 does not constitute clear and convincing proof of the state's inability to protect its citizens, since no state can guarantee the protection of all its citizens at all times. Local failures to provide effective policing do not amount to a lack of state protection unless they are part of a broader pattern of the state's inability to provide protection.14 The burden of proof that rests on the claimant increases with the level of democracy of the state in question. The more democratic a state is, the more the claimant must have done to exhaust all courses of action open to them to demonstrate state protection was or would not be forthcoming.15 When the state in question is a democratic state, the claimant must do more than simply show that he or she went to see some members of the police force and that his or her efforts were unsuccessful.16

Mexico is a democratic country, with functioning political and judicial systems and an official apparatus sufficient to provide a measure of protection to its citizens. Thus the burden on the claimant to seek protection from the state agencies of the country is a high one which he should have first attempted prior to seeking international protection.17 The state authorities do and will take steps to protect victims of crime and corruption. For example, documentary evidence18 indicates that the Mexican Government continues to push forward with federal police reform by focusing on rigorous new recruiting, training and vetting measures. The Federal Preventive Police (PFP) has internal regulations with disciplinary measures that classify transgressors and apply sanctions, including removal, suspension or dismissal. To enforce police internal rules, a collegiate organ, headed by Internal Affairs General Coordinator, decides whether there is responsibility or not. The Attorney General's Office (PGR) provides three offices to control its members. The first office is in charge of testing the institution's public officials' adherence to legality, professionalism and impartiality. More importantly, the Mexican security forces are described as hierarchical, and a complainant can seek redress at a higher level if dissatisfied with the services at the local level.

The documentary19 evidence indicates that Mexico is not in a state of collapse, and further, has been making and continues to make serious efforts to fight crime and corruption. All 31 states in Mexico maintain a preventive and judicial police force. There are at least 350,000 police personnel spread across 3,000 police forces at various judicial levels, although some estimates are that the federal, state, and municipal police forces included approximately 500,000 agents. The judicial police are the law enforcement branch of the state-level Public Ministry (MP), the Attorney General's Office (PGJ) is responsible for investigating and prosecuting local criminal offences, and the Federal Preventative Police (PFP) maintain order and security. The coordination for Federal Support Forces contains special operations and emergency response and the Regional Security Coordination supervises 34 regional commands. The military is responsible for external security but also has significant domestic security responsibilities, particularly in combating drug trafficking and maintaining order, a role that has been increased significantly over the years due to military training and the perception that it is relatively free of corruption. The country also has a number of other state agencies that address criminality, including drug trafficking, kidnapping and corruption in an effort to assist citizens to obtain state protection.

Documentary20 evidence also indicates that in 2008, Mexico made unprecedented efforts and achieved unprecedented results in attacking the corrosive effects of drug trafficking and consumption during the first complete year of the Calderon Administration. Significant Mexican counter-narcotics enforcement actions in 2007 included sophisticated organized crime investigations, marijuana and poppy eradication, strong bilateral cooperation on drug interdiction and the arrests of several major drug traffickers. In 2008, the Bureau for International Narcotics and Law Enforcement Affairs' (INL) Narcotics Assistance Section (NAS) Professionalization and Training Program drew on interagency support from Department of Justice (DOJ) and Department of Homeland Security (DHS) agencies to provide 294 specialized training courses to 8,112 Mexican law enforcement and prosecutors at the federal and state level, with courses on criminal investigations, crime scene search and preservation of evidence, cyber-crimes, explosives and incendiary devices, highway and airport interdiction, and counterterrorism. In 2008, Mexican law enforcement seized over 19 metric tons (MT) of cocaine, 1,650 MT of marijuana, 168 kilograms (kg) of opium gum, 192 kg of heroin, and 341 kg of methamphetamine. In most categories, this was a reduction by half from last year. U.S. law enforcement agencies attribute this reduction to better enforcement which has forced traffickers to seek alternate routes or alternative enterprises. As of November 12, 2008, GOM security forces had seized 39,437 illegal firearms, including the record-breaking seizure of weapons believed to belong to the Zetas of the Gulf cartel, and arrested 26,947 persons on drug-related charges-26,571 Mexicans and 376 foreigners. Cooperation with the government of the USA is touted as key in the fight against drugs and drug related crime. Mexico's current administration is dedicated to pursuing cooperation with the USA to fight their common problem. From January 2000 through September 2006, the Mexican government arrested over 79,000 people on charges related to drug trafficking.21 Of these arrests, some 78,831 are low level drug dealers. Mexico also arrested 15 cartel leaders, 74 lieutenants, 53 financial officers, and 428 hitmen. In January 2007, Mexico extradited 15 persons wanted for prosecution in the United States, including four senior drug traffickers. The drug traffickers included Osiel Cardenas Guillen, the alleged head of the powerful Gulf cartel. All this indicates Mexico is making serious effort to combat organized crime and drug trafficking.

Although corruption is an ongoing problem in Mexico, anticorruption efforts continue. Under the Fox administration all agencies, departments and government institutions, including the Mexican military, were asked to adhere to strict enforcement of anticorruption measures.22 Corruption remains a considerable hurdle for Mexico in reforming institutions and confronting criminal gangs whose assets run in the billions of dollars. On October 27, Attorney General Medina Mora announced that five senior officials from the PGR's anti-organized crime unit (SIEDO) had been arrested for passing information to a major drug cartel. On October 31, Acting Federal Police (PFP) Commissioner Gerardo Garay Cardena resigned over allegations of his connections to the Sinaloa drug cartel; subsequently, he was arrested on corruption charges. Dozens more junior federal security officials have also been suspended or fired over corruption charges.23 In June 2007, the government of Mexico suspended 284 police officers from the PFP and AFI, including 34 state and Federal District police chiefs pending probes into their possible links to organized crime or drug trafficking.24 All these actions indicate that Mexico is making serious effort to combat corruption.

The claimant was questioned as to what efforts he made to seek state protection before fleeing Mexico. The claimant testified that he did not go to the police at all. The claimant was asked why he did not approach the police. He said it was because he was afraid due to the fact that members of Los Zetas had warned him not to go to the police because the police worked with Los Zetas. The claimant was asked if he believed that the police worked for Los Zetas. He responded that the news often reported that the police worked for Los Zetas. The claimant was asked if it was his understanding or belief that the entire police force worked for Los Zetas or only a particular level of police. The claimant explained that he believed that it was the municipal and ministerial police as a whole that worked for Los Zetas. The claimant furnished no persuasive evidence to show that Los Zetas has infiltrated the entire police force at both the municipal and ministerial levels or for that matter that Los Zetas controls high levels of those police forces in their entirety. The claimant was asked if he had considered going to the federal police for assistance. He said that had not considered this option because he believed that if he had approached the federal police, they would have immediately responded by conducting a raid of the area where his business was located, which would in turn have tipped off Los Zetas to the fact that he had gone to the authorities to make a complaint about them. The claimant was asked if he believed that the federal police were in a position to have offered him any kind of protection. He responded in the negative. The claimant was asked why he believed this to be the case. He responded by saying that all the federal police would have been in a position to do for him was conduct searches and raids, but would not be able to offer him an armed police officer to guard him. I find that it is not reasonable for the claimant to expect the federal police to assign a body guard to offer him 24-hour around the clock protection. Not even the best staffed and best resourced police force anywhere in the world would be able to guarantee someone's protection against criminal threats at all times and in all places. The claimant was asked if he believed that the federal police would give him any protection whatsoever. He responded by saying that he believed that they would not be able to provide him with any protection. The claimant was asked why he believed this to be the case. The claimant responded by saying that perhaps the federal police might be able to protect him for two to three weeks and that after that he would be on his own. The claimant was asked if he considering going to any other state agency in the government for protection. His answer was that he gave it no consideration. He was asked if that was the case. He testified that he did not want the problem to escalate. The claimant was asked to explain what he meant by this. He said that if he went to a higher level of police, he did not want the situation to become more complicated.

I find, on a balance of probabilities, that the claimant and his family did not make diligent efforts, nor did they take all reasonable steps to obtain protection from the authorities regarding the death threats made against him and his family; the kidnapping and torture that he suffered at their hands, in addition to the extortion of his business by members of Los Zetas. Furthermore, I find that it was not objectively reasonable for the claimant and his family not to have made any efforts whatsoever to approach federal law enforcement agencies for protection. One of the reasons why, according to the claimant, he did not approach any authorities in Mexico for protection before leaving the country was that corrupt police officers and government officials worked for Los Zetas. The claimant offered no persuasive evidence to show that all levels of the municipal, state, or federal police have been infiltrated by Los Zetas or that Los Zetas has completely taken control of policing by all police forces or that they have substantially undermined policing operations at all levels of the police force in Mexico. The claimant made it clear in his testimony that he did not believe that the federal police had been corrupted through infiltration by Los Zetas. On the contrary, the claimant testified that had he gone to the federal police that they would have responded by launching raids and searches in the area where he operated his business. I find that this is indicative of the fact that federal authorities are willing and able to take direct and significant actions against criminal organizations and organizations involved in drug trafficking such as Los Zetas. Documentary evidence indicates that in July 2006, local police in the southern state of Tabasco unknowingly arrested Mateo Diaz Lopez, believed to be a leader of the Zetas.25 Further documentary evidence26 indicates that violent drug traffickers had infiltrated the police force, Mexican soldiers disarmed 149 local policemen assigned to the municipality of Rosario, Baja California, on December 28. Besides stripping local policemen of their weapons, the Baja California State Office of the Attorney General ordered all its Rosario personnel reassigned to other posts including Tijuana and Ensenada. In April 2007 over 100 state police officers in the northern state of Nuevo Leon were suspended due to corruption concerns. In June 2007, President Calderon purged 284 federal police commanders, including federal commanders of all 31 states and the federal district.27 These commanders were suspended and subjected to drug and polygraph tests. The Mexican government immediately named replacements for the 284 dismissed commanders. I find that this documentary evidence illustrates that Mexican authorities are making serious efforts to fight crime and corruption that exists within the police force and to bring police officers who have links with Los Zetas and drug trafficking to justice.

I would be remiss if I did not acknowledge and consider that there is information in the documentation to indicate that inefficiency, bribery and corruption remain issues in Mexican security forces at all levels, as well as within the public service sector. However, weighted against this is persuasive evidence that indicates that Mexico candidly acknowledges its past problems and is making serious efforts to rectify the corruption and impunity that exists.

The Board accepts that Mexico has had some difficulties in the past with addressing the criminality and corruption that exist within the security forces in Mexico. However, the panel assigns a greater probative value to the documentary evidence than to the claimant's opinion with respect to the adequacy of state protection. The documentary evidence cited is drawn from a variety of reliable and independent sources.

The Board recognizes that there are some inconsistencies among several sources within the documentary evidence; however, the preponderance of the objective evidence regarding current country conditions suggests that, although not perfect, there is an adequate state protection in Mexico for victims of crime, that Mexico is making serious and genuine efforts to address the problem of criminality, and that the police are both willing and able to protect victims. Police corruption and deficiencies, although existing and noted by the Board, are not generalized. I am of the view in perusing the documentary evidence, that, as a whole, the issues of corruption and deficiencies are being addressed by the state of Mexico.

I find that the claimants, in the circumstances of this case, have failed to rebut the presumption of state protection with clear and convincing evidence. Therefore, I am not persuaded that the state of Mexico would not be reasonably forthcoming with state protection, should the claimants seek it.

As the claims of his wife and children rely entirely on the evidence of the claimant and no persuasive evidence was adduced to differentiate their claims from that of the claimant, the claims of his wife and children must also fail.

I determine that the claimant and his family are neither Convention refugees nor persons in need of protection. The Refugee Protection Division therefore rejects their claims.
